summary:
Firewatch is a web platform that turns NASA satellite data into practical wildfire monitoring for Mozambique’s 25 protected areas: 8 national parks, 4 wildlife reserves and 13 forest reserves.

The problem: fire is part of the African landscape, but too much fire, or fire at the wrong time, destroys habitats, wildlife and forests that take years to grow. Many of these areas are vast and hard to patrol on the ground.

What we built: Firewatch pulls real thermal detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, MODIS on Aqua and Terra) every 5 minutes, and adds NASA EONET events and Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery from Microsoft Planetary Computer. Everything appears on an interactive map with a calendar, history and VIIRS–MODIS cross-matching. Teams can set email alerts by area and minimum fire power, export CSV and GeoJSON to work offline, and keep an encrypted field-verification log.

Firewatch does not predict or confirm fires. It shows rangers where to look first, and confirmation happens on the ground. It uses real data only, with no simulated records, and it is live now.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Firewatch is a web platform that helps park managers and rangers in Mozambique see where satellites are detecting heat inside 25 protected areas: 8 national parks, 4 wildlife reserves and 13 forest reserves (Gorongosa is the default view). Every 5 minutes it requests real thermal detections from NASA FIRMS (VIIRS on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, MODIS on Aqua and Terra) with a single request for all of Mozambique, then filters them locally by protected area. It adds NASA EONET wildfire events and Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery from Microsoft Planetary Computer for context.

Users can explore an interactive map with filters by satellite, area and minimum fire power, a calendar that flags unusually active days (above the mean plus one standard deviation), a historical analysis, and a VIIRS–MODIS cross-matching tool that links detections within 1.5 km and 12 hours without ever deleting the original records. Teams can create email alerts for chosen areas and power levels, and export data as CSV or GeoJSON to work offline. A private field-verification module lets rangers record what they found on the ground, with encrypted offline drafts and separate satellite and field coordinates.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Many conservation areas are huge and hard to patrol. Firewatch shortens the time between a satellite detection and a team knowing where to look, helps prioritise the strongest hotspots, and builds a history that supports planning. Between 15 October and 14 November 2026 it processed 2,989 detections across Mozambique. Our aim is to support, never replace, the people who protect wildlife and forests.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Data: NASA FIRMS, NASA EONET, Microsoft Planetary Computer (Sentinel-2, Landsat) and Gmail SMTP for alerts. Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn and SQLite. Frontend: Node 20 and Vite. Deployment: Docker and Docker Compose, Caddy with automatic HTTPS (Let’s Encrypt), Amazon Web Services (EC2, Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS), GitHub and a free sslip.io domain. Development support: GitHub Copilot for code refactoring. No special hardware is needed: the platform runs on a single cloud server and works in any web browser.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a generic fire map, Firewatch combines two satellite families with different strengths (VIIRS for detail, MODIS for long history), cross-matches them, and closes the loop with a private field-verification workflow. The interface is in Portuguese for local users, and boundary quality is reported for each area.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: a heat hotspot is not a confirmed fire, and the platform never predicts or confirms fires on its own. Clouds, smoke, agricultural burns, the delay of about 3 hours and the 375 m / 1 km pixel size are stated limits.

- Real data only: if a data key is missing, feeds stay unavailable instead of showing generated records.

- Boundary quality: each area reports its source and quality. Two areas (the partial Lake Niassa reserve and Pomene) use approximate extents that must be confirmed with the authorities.

- Privacy: field notes and GPS positions are private and never appear in public exports.

- Simplicity and cost: one cloud server that is easy to redeploy and maintain.

- Future work: an AI assistant is on the roadmap but intentionally deferred until the core science is validated.
